in_text_mentions: ia‐like subtype being the most prevalent, accounting for 18 cases (38%). This form was characterized by edematous borders and purpuric dots, which were evident on dermoscopy and attributed to extravasated erythrocytes (Figure 1a–d). Other subtypes included papulonodular (12 cases, 25%; Figure 1e–g), vesiculobullous (10 cases, 21%; Figure 2a), granuloma annulare‐like (5 cases, 10%; Figure 2b, c), and cellulitis‐like (3 cases, 6%; Figure 2d). Pruritus was a common symptom, affecting 96% of the patients, while systemic symptoms such as fever, malaise, and arthralgia were reported in 16% of cases.

abnormalities were identified in our cohort. Peripheral eosinophilia, defined as an eosinophil count ≥ 0.5 × 109/l, was present in 29 patients (60%), and leukocytosis (≥ 11 × 109/l) was observed in 15 patients (31%). Histopathological examination revealed eosinophilic infiltration in the superficial and deep dermis in all cases, along with the characteristic “flame figures” in 34 patients (71%) (Figure 2e). Granulomatous infiltration was less common, observed in 10% of cases, but its presence underscores the histopathological diversity of WS and its overlap with other granulomatous disorders.

panels.figure_caption: Histopathologic findings of Wells syndrome (hematoxylin and eosin stain, 400× magnification). Superficial and mid-dermal interstitial and perivascular eosinophil-rich inflammatory infiltrates accompanied by dermal edema and eosinophilic degranulation. No evidence of leukocytoclastic vasculitis was identified.
in_text_mentions: pheral eosinophilia, and lack of sustained response to antibiotic therapy, a punch biopsy of an active lesion was performed. Histopathologic examination demonstrated superficial and mid-dermal interstitial and perivascular eosinophil-rich inflammatory infiltrates admixed with lymphocytes, accompanied by prominent dermal edema and eosinophilic degranulation. No evidence of leukocytoclastic vasculitis was identified. Although flame figures were not conspicuous, the overall histopathologic findings, in correlation with the clinical presentation, supported a diagnosis of Wells syndrome (Figure 2).

in_text_mentions: examination of the skin, there were multiple violaceous, indurated, nontender papules coalescing into a plaque with clustered nodules and central crusting on the occipital scalp. Haematoxylin and Eosin (H&E) stains demonstrated dense inflammation with predominate eosinophils and some neutrophils in higher manifestations (Figure 1). There is secondary reactive fibroblast/fibrohistocystic features and vascular ectasias but no vasculitis. Periodic acid‐Schiff (PAS), Grocott methenamine silver (GMS), and Gram and acid‐fast stains were negative. There were also no histologic features of malignancy.

in_text_mentions: terium tuberculosis and fungal culture were negative. Lymph node biopsy showed lymph node architecture effaced by diffuse and nodular infiltrate of large cells with high mitotic activity suggestive of diffuse large B cell lymphoma (Figure 2A). Immunohistochemistry on the cervical lymph node showed lymphomatous infiltrate positive for CD20, c-Myc (90%), and MUM 1(90%) with a Ki 67 index of 85-90% (Figures 2B, 2C, 2D). Skin biopsy showed sub-epidermal separation and marked dermal edema (Figure 3A). Eosinophilic infiltrates around vessels and flame figures suggest Wells syndrome (Figures 3B, 3C).

plate_findings.evidence: Large erythematous infiltrated plaque involving the lateral thigh with poorly demarcated borders

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Clinical photograph of a real patient showing a large erythematous infiltrated plaque with poorly demarcated borders and edema on the lateral thigh, explicitly captioned as Wells syndrome (eosinophilic cellulitis) and resembling cellulitis. Disease attribution is supported by the panel-specific caption and the disease-focused article title. The article title describes an elderly patient, supporting older_adult; visible skin is light. b: Clinical photograph of a real patient showing a confluent erythematous plaque with irregular margins and surrounding edema on the medial thigh, explicitly captioned as the bilateral cellulitis-like eruption characteristic of Wells syndrome (eosinophilic cellulitis). Disease attribution is supported by the panel-specific caption and the disease-focused article title. The article title describes an elderly patient, supporting older_adult; visible skin is light.

panels.figure_caption: Clinical presentation of Wells syndrome. (a) Large erythematous infiltrated plaque involving the lateral thigh with poorly demarcated borders and associated edema, clinically resembling cellulitis. (b) Confluent erythematous plaque involving the medial thigh with irregular margins and surrounding edema, demonstrating the bilateral cellulitis-like eruption characteristic of Wells syndrome.
in_text_mentions: Physical examination revealed erythematous infiltrated plaques involving the bilateral upper and lower extremities, with associated pitting edema and overlying dry, flaking skin (Figure 1). No palpable lymphadenopathy was identified, and the remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.
